safety_note: The prescribed dose, treatment decision and local urgent-contact plan take priority. Call 112 or 999 for severe breathing difficulty, severe chest pain, collapse, a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow your oncology unit’s written urgent-contact plan for other new or worsening symptoms; do not wait for the next appointment.

anatomy_note: The established anatomical illustration links body areas to the full regimen-specific descriptions. A body location helps explain possible effects; it does not diagnose the cause of a symptom or indicate its frequency.
title: Vemurafenib alone — advanced melanoma
purpose: To control advanced BRAF V600-mutated melanoma with a daily oral targeted medicine; benefit and tolerability are reviewed for the individual.
schedule_summary: Vemurafenib twice daily, about 12 hours apart, every day. A 28-day review cycle does not mean a planned tablet-free week.
scope_note: This is vemurafenib monotherapy. It is not the cobimetinib combination and has no cobimetinib seven-day break. The team must plan any radiotherapy because BRAF treatment can increase radiation-related reactions.
indication_text: Adults with unresectable or metastatic melanoma and a confirmed BRAF V600 tumour mutation.
phases_note: Vemurafenib twice daily, about 12 hours apart, every day. A 28-day review cycle does not mean a planned tablet-free week.
timeline_note: This is a reference schedule. Your prescribed dose, blood results, symptoms and the team’s written plan determine whether treatment goes ahead.
consent_support: Discuss the exact diagnosis and treatment intent, expected benefit and uncertainty, alternatives, regimen-specific risks, tests, fertility, practical burdens and your preferences. This guide supports the consent conversation and does not replace it. This is vemurafenib monotherapy. It is not the cobimetinib combination and has no cobimetinib seven-day break. The team must plan any radiotherapy because BRAF treatment can increase radiation-related reactions.
urgent_extra: Contact the oncology team promptly for fainting or palpitations, eye pain or blurred vision, a blistering or rapidly spreading rash, severe sunburn, persistent vomiting or diarrhoea, reduced urine or yellow skin or eyes. Report new or changing skin growths even when the melanoma is responding.

agents.name: Vemurafenib
agents.explanation: Vemurafenib blocks the altered BRAF V600 protein that can drive melanoma-cell growth. A confirmed tumour BRAF V600 result is needed. Healthy tissues can also be affected; tablets need the same careful monitoring as treatment given in hospital.
agents.watch: Report new skin growths, sunburn-like reactions, eye pain or blurred vision, palpitations or fainting.
risks: Photosensitivity, rash and new skin cancers

passport_visit_note: Record the dose actually taken or administered, symptoms, tests and agreed next step. A planned or held visit is not a completed treatment dose.
anatomy: Headache and tiredness can occur. New severe headache, confusion, collapse or neurological changes need urgent assessment rather than attribution to tablets.
Eye pain, redness, light sensitivity or blurred vision can signal inflammation. Report promptly for eye assessment.
The electrical rhythm can change; ECG and blood chemistry checks help detect risk. Palpitations or fainting need prompt assessment.
Photosensitivity, rash and new skin cancers can occur. Protect skin and report new growths; blistering or peeling is urgent.
Blood tests check for liver injury. Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or severe upper-abdominal discomfort need prompt review.
Kidney injury or dehydration can affect dosing. Report reduced urine or inability to keep fluids down.
Joint or muscle pain can affect daily activities. Tell the team if pain limits walking or self-care, or occurs with marked weakness.
Nausea, diarrhoea and reduced appetite can cause dehydration. Keep the agreed symptom plan and report persistent or severe symptoms.

chronology_notes.title: Schedule and review
chronology_notes.text: Vemurafenib twice daily, about 12 hours apart, every day. A 28-day review cycle does not mean a planned tablet-free week.

chronology_notes.title: Holds, missed treatment and phase changes
chronology_notes.text: Take a missed dose only if at least four hours remain before the next dose. Otherwise skip it. Do not double a dose. If you vomit after taking it, do not take an extra dose; take the next dose at the usual time. Contact the team if vomiting continues or treatment has been held.

administration_text: The usual starting dose is 960 mg twice daily, about 12 hours apart; the prescribed dose may differ after review. Swallow tablets whole with water. Vemurafenib can be taken with or without food, but do not regularly take both daily doses on an empty stomach. Keep a consistent routine and follow the pharmacy label.
monitoring_summary: Confirm BRAF V600, blood count, kidney/liver tests, medicine interactions and skin assessment. Current Zelboraf product information calls for a baseline ECG and electrolytes including magnesium for all patients; this supplements the NCCP risk-based ECG row. Staging scans establish the sites of melanoma. Blood count, kidney and liver tests before each cycle. NCCP specifies ECG every four weeks for the first 12 weeks, then every 12 weeks and after dose changes. Its skin-review row states week eight then every 12 weeks; current Zelboraf product information instead requires monthly prescriber skin examinations. The team should supply a reconciled written skin-check plan using the current product information. Current Zelboraf product information calls for monthly skin checks during treatment and for up to six months after stopping, or until another anticancer therapy starts. Head-and-neck checks every three months and chest CT every six months during treatment screen for other cancers; these are distinct from the individual melanoma-response scan plan. Anal/pelvic checks are considered at baseline/end and when indicated. Record the team’s coordinated surveillance plan rather than duplicating scans.

support.title: Supportive medicines and symptom plan
support.text: This is a minimal-emetic-risk oral regimen in the NCCP plan. Anti-sickness medicine is chosen to match symptoms and interactions; do not add over-the-counter medicines without checking. Agree a hydration and diarrhoea plan, and report inability to drink or persistent symptoms.

support.title: Skin and daily care
support.text: Use broad-spectrum UVA/UVB sun protection, protective clothing and lip protection; the product information specifies SPF 30 or higher. Sun sensitivity can be marked. Check skin regularly for new growths or changes, and keep scheduled dermatology reviews.

support.title: Fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding
support.text: Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least six months after the final dose. Vemurafenib may reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraception, so ask for an appropriate alternative or additional method. Discuss fertility and breastfeeding before treatment; tell the team immediately if pregnancy is possible.

evidence.title: What the treatment evidence can and cannot tell you
evidence.intro: Evidence needs to match the medicine, dose combination, disease stage and previous treatment.
evidence.population: 675 previously untreated patients with metastatic BRAF V600E melanoma
evidence.interpretation: At the 2011 analysis, six-month overall survival was 84% versus 64%; response was 48% versus 5%. These are group results from that study, not a prediction for you.
limitations: Early historical analysis; later crossover and subsequent treatment affect longer-term comparisons.
Dacarbazine comparator, not a modern BRAF/MEK combination or checkpoint regimen.
Personal benefit depends on the cancer, previous treatment, general health and the available alternatives.

chapters.title: Understanding your diagnosis and treatment goal
chapters.intro: Use your own pathology, stage and agreed plan alongside this guide.

items.title: Your diagnosis and stage
items.text: Keep the pathology report, original melanoma site, stage and known sites of spread. This guide concerns advanced disease that cannot be removed completely by surgery or has spread; it does not describe a postoperative recurrence-prevention course.

items.title: The tumour test
items.text: A BRAF V600 test helps identify whether BRAF-targeted medicines are an option. A tumour mutation does not by itself mean an inherited family condition. Keep the exact result and ask how it changes your choices.

items.title: Scans and local treatments
items.text: Record the scans used to follow known disease. Surgery or radiotherapy may have a separate role for a particular site; ask for their timing and risks to be added to the overall plan.

items.title: New changes still matter
items.text: Report a new lump, changing mole, persistent skin sore or unexplained symptom. A response at one site does not establish that every other symptom is harmless.

items.title: Other medicines
items.text: Give the team a complete list of prescribed, over-the-counter and herbal medicines, supplements and allergies. Ask before adding a new medicine; treatment interactions and symptom-masking can matter.

items.title: Practical arrangements
items.text: Know where and when bloods are taken, how results reach the prescriber, and how to obtain the next supply or appointment. Ask for written instructions in a format you can use without a phone.

chapters.title: Tests, results and treatment decisions
chapters.intro: Safety tests and scans answer different questions.

items.title: What a result means
items.text: Ask which result is abnormal, whether the finding needs a repeat test and whether treatment is held, changed or stopped. Do not use a reference range or one normal result to decide independently that a dose is safe.

chapters.title: What to expect between visits
chapters.intro: A quiet treatment day does not rule out later problems.

items.title: Act on new symptoms
items.text: Contact the oncology team promptly for fainting or palpitations, eye pain or blurred vision, a blistering or rapidly spreading rash, severe sunburn, persistent vomiting or diarrhoea, reduced urine or yellow skin or eyes. Report new or changing skin growths even when the melanoma is responding.

items.title: A useful daily record
items.text: Record symptoms, temperature when unwell, bowel changes, fluid intake when reduced, missed doses and any medicines used for relief. Note how symptoms affect eating, walking, sleep and normal activities; this helps the team judge severity.

items.title: When life is affected
items.text: Tell the team about fatigue, pain, appetite, sleep, mood and ability to work or care for others. Practical and supportive care can accompany anticancer treatment; you do not have to wait until treatment ends.

chapters.title: Skin, body changes and daily care
chapters.intro: Use the detailed body map to locate symptoms, not to diagnose them.

items.title: Skin and sun
items.text: Use broad-spectrum UVA/UVB sun protection, protective clothing and lip protection; the product information specifies SPF 30 or higher. Sun sensitivity can be marked. Check skin regularly for new growths or changes, and keep scheduled dermatology reviews.

items.title: The body map
items.text: The organ anchors show possible locations and warning symptoms. They do not show how common each effect is, and a symptom may have another cause. New symptoms should be assessed in their clinical context.

items.title: Food, fluids and activity
items.text: Keep meals and fluids manageable and follow any individual fluid or diet restrictions. Gentle activity and rest can be adjusted to how you feel. Ask for dietetic or rehabilitation help if intake, weight, strength or mobility is falling.

items.title: Keep checking the plan
items.text: A new medicine, fever, hospital admission, procedure or radiotherapy may change treatment timing. Tell the oncology team and take the wallet card or medicine list to other appointments.

chapters.title: Fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding
chapters.intro: Discuss these issues before the first dose whenever possible.

items.title: Contraception and pregnancy
items.text: Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least six months after the final dose. Vemurafenib may reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraception, so ask for an appropriate alternative or additional method. Discuss fertility and breastfeeding before treatment; tell the team immediately if pregnancy is possible.

items.title: Fertility preservation
items.text: Ask whether treatment or the cancer may affect fertility and whether fertility preservation is appropriate before treatment. A change in periods or sexual function does not reliably establish infertility.

items.title: Written dates and methods
items.text: Record the agreed method, last treatment date and how long precautions continue. Different medicines have different intervals, so ask for clarification after a switch or combination change.

items.title: Sexual health
items.text: Tell the team about sexual symptoms, relationship concerns or practical difficulties with the agreed precautions. Ask for a private discussion and specialist support when needed.

chapters.title: Decisions, support and useful records
chapters.intro: Your priorities belong in the treatment discussion.

items.title: Benefits and alternatives
items.text: Ask what the treatment aims to achieve, what alternatives are suitable, how likely important benefits are in your situation and how treatment burden or uncertainty affects that choice. A trial average cannot promise an individual outcome.

items.title: Support alongside treatment
items.text: Ask about symptom control, psychological support, finances, transport, work and help at home. Palliative or supportive care can be used alongside anticancer treatment to improve comfort and function.

items.title: A person you trust
items.text: If helpful, bring a family member or supporter and agree what information may be shared. Ask for an interpreter or accessible information when needed; use teach-back to check the schedule and urgent plan.

items.title: Your document set
items.text: Keep consent information, the three-page summary, complete handbook, treatment card, test plan and real contact details together. The QR opens more information but essential instructions remain available in print.

chapters.title: After a treatment hold, change or completion
chapters.intro: The next step should be written down, not assumed.

items.title: A treatment summary
items.text: Record medicines and doses received, important side effects, admissions, last-dose date, ongoing symptom treatment and the clinician responsible for follow-up. Ask for an updated paper copy for your GP and other treating teams.

items.title: Your next review
items.text: Confirm the next blood test, scan and review, who explains the result, and which symptoms should trigger contact sooner. Keep actual daytime and out-of-hours numbers accessible after treatment stops.
